Where overgrazing has altered plant community composition, blue grama (Bouteloua gracilis), needle leaf sedge (Carex filifolia), bluegrass and/or prairie junegrass (Koeleria cristata) may be dominant species.
A wide variety of forb species occur depending on soils and grazing history. Among the more common forbs are low ragweed (Ambrosia artemisifolia), yarrow (Achillea millefolium), sweetclover Melilotus officinale), fringed sage (Artemisia frigida), cudleaf sage (Artemisia ludoviciana), aster (Aster, sp.), chickweed (Cerastrium arvense), narrow-leaved collomia (Collomia linearis), rush skeletonweed (Lygodesmia juncea), and scurfpea (Psoralea sp.).
A variety of grassland - shrub types occur in the Project Area.

Silver sagebrush (Artemisia cana) occurs primarily on relatively level terrain and along drainage bottoms on clayey or loamy soils. Big sagebrush (Artemisia tridentata) is relatively uncommon and is found primarily on more heavily textured upland soils. Skunkbush sumac (Rhus trilobata) is characteristic of well drained scoria and sandy soils on dry south and west facing slopes. Greasewood (Sarcobatus vermiculatus) is present on a very limited area of alluvial soil on the extreme northern portion of Tract III. The shadscale saltbush (Atriplex confertifolia)-rubber rabbitbrush (Chrysothamnus nauseosus) type is characteristic of severe, eroded slopes often with localized aikali conditions.
